summary: This note summarizes Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel The Handmaid's Tale, set in the Republic of Gilead, a totalitarian Christian theonomy in a near-future New England that overthrew the United States government. It follows the handmaid Offred, whose name derives from the possessive form 'of Fred', and explores women's subjugation and the ways they gain independence. The note also mentions that the title echoes the structure of Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales. The source is a repetitive draft with several near-identical paragraphs.
one_line: Margaret Atwood's 1985 dystopian novel about the handmaid Offred in the theocratic Republic of Gilead, formerly the United States.
key_facts: The Handmaid's Tale is a 1985 dystopian novel by Canadian author Margaret Atwood.
The novel is set in a near-future New England.
The setting is a totalitarian, Christian theonomy that has overthrown the United States government.
The novel explores themes of women in subjugation and the various means by which they gain individualism and independence.
The novel's title echoes the component parts of Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, which is a series of connected stories.
The title echoes parts such as "The Merchant's Tale" and "The Parson's Tale".
The novel focuses on the journey of the handmaid Offred.
The name Offred derives from the possessive form "of Fred".
Handmaids are forbidden to use their birth names and must echo the male, or master, whom they serve.
The Handmaid's Tale is set in the Republic of Gilead.
The Republic of Gilead is described as a theonomic military dictatorship.
Gilead was formed within the borders of what was formerly the United States of America.
